# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# A Careful Reading of the Two-Year Follow-up

This report moves the debate forward more than any of the previous four documents:

- It tests the novelty question within one trial over time, rather than by comparing different studies.
- It adds a stricter measure of hours.
- It runs the meetings test under a registered plan.
- It finds that the meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which explains the "no decay" claim.
- It reports a failed arm and reversions openly.

Its overall picture is credible. The per-hour gain is about 8 to 10%, it is fading modestly, and a large part runs through cutting meetings.

There are still problems. The summary mixes hours measures. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result. The control offices were contaminated in a way that affects the decay estimate. And it is unclear what the system-log hours actually include.

## Checking the numbers

- **Varden at 24 months.** 0.966 ÷ 0.88 gives +9.8% per hour on timesheets, and 0.966 ÷ 0.89 gives +8.5% on logs. Both match.
- **Halden continuers.** Hours of 34.9 ÷ 40.3 give a ratio of 0.866, which is −13.4%. Output of 96.8 ÷ 0.866 gives +11.8%. Both match.
- **Mediation shares.** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100. Consistent.
- **Counter-arm costs.** Output per FTE fell 11.4%. Restoring it needs roughly 1 ÷ 0.886, or about 13% more staff. That fits the county's estimate of 12%. A 9% rise in cost per contact is plausible if staff are about three-quarters of cost.
- **The Halden baseline of 40.3 needs checking.** That is exactly the Varga–Holm baseline for all 27 time-tracking organisations. Their 17-organisation subset had 40.4. The baseline should come from these 11 organisations' own time tracking, and it isn't clear whether all 11 have it. Using a borrowed baseline would make the 11.8% figure unreliable.

## What the report gets right

1. **The decay is measured within the trial.** Comparing like with like on timesheets, the gain fell from +12.5% to +9.8%, a decline of about a fifth to a quarter. This is the evidence the meta-analysis lacked. It also contradicts "no decay" without supporting "fades to zero."
2. **The meta-analysis's duration claim is corrected.** The four long studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. So their +14% reflects inflated designs and says nothing about decay.
3. **There is now a controlled comparison for counter offices.** Waiting times were 7.3 minutes in treated offices against 4.0 in controls in months 10 to 12. The county ended the arm on cost grounds, which turns "output per worker falls" into a concrete cost: 12% more staff and 9% higher cost per contact.
4. **Quality is better covered.** At 24 months, appeal overturns (3.2% against 3.0%) cover decisions that have had time to be appealed. This addresses the time-lag concern I raised about the nine-month report.
5. **The limits are clearly stated.** The Halden continuers are called "survivors twice over," and their figures are presented as an upper bound. The two control offices that cut meetings are explicitly not overclaimed.

## Problems

### 1. The summary mixes hours measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% is based on timesheets and the 8.5% on system logs. The like-for-like decline is 12.5% to 9.8%. The body gets this right, but the summary makes the decay look larger than the trial shows.

The change is also not tested formally. The nine-month interval (+6.9 to +18.4) and the 24-month interval (+4.6 to +15.2) overlap heavily. "Consistent with some fading" is fair. A within-trial test of whether the decline is real should be reported.

### 2. Contamination of the control group probably exaggerates the decay

Two of the seven control offices cut meetings at month 15. Their output per hour then rose about 4% against their own earlier figures. If that held through to month 24, the control group's average would rise by roughly 1 percentage point. The difference-in-differences would shrink by the same amount, about 1 percentage point.

That could account for a third or more of the 2.7-point decline on timesheets. The exact size depends on office sizes and on which months the 24-month estimate covers. Some of the apparent fading may therefore be the control group improving, not the treatment wearing off. The report draws on this episode for its argument about reorganising without cutting hours, but not when interpreting the decay. It should report the estimate with these two offices excluded, as a sensitivity check.

### 3. The control-office meeting figures don't obviously fit together

Control offices' meeting time went from 7.2 to 7.0 hours, an average fall of 0.2. But two of the seven offices reportedly fell by 2.1 hours each. That alone would pull the average down by about 0.6 hours.

So one of three things happened:

- the other five control offices *increased* their meetings by about 0.4 hours each;
- meetings crept back in the two audited offices by month 24;
- the figures are weighted by staff in a way that changes the picture.

The second possibility matters most: if meetings creep back, any gain from cutting them may not last. The report should clarify which explanation applies.

### 4. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result

- **The hypothesis came from the same offices.** The mediation plan was registered at month 11, after the nine-month exploratory correlation in these same offices. The test was set out in advance, which counts for something, but the sample is not independent. It is still 7 treated offices.
- **More office-months does not mean more independent evidence.** The report cites "a larger sample of office-months," but repeated months from the same office are not independent observations. With 14 clusters, an interval of 28 to 66% for the meetings share looks optimistic. The report should state how the intervals account for clustering.
- **Meeting cuts were not randomised.** The reduced schedule was randomised; the size of each office's meeting cut was not. Offices whose managers cut meetings more may differ in other ways, such as better management overall. That is the same confounding concern raised about the r = 0.71 correlation. The limitations section acknowledges this assumption, but it should temper the language in the summary.
- **The two mediators are connected.** Fewer meetings may also reduce fatigue. How the effect is split between the two pathways then depends on how the model orders them, which the report does not describe.

"Supports" would be accurate. "Confirms" is not. The finding is still meaningful: the meetings pathway was set out in advance, its interval excludes zero, and it is larger than the fatigue pathway.

### 5. What do system logs measure?

"Active log-in time on the case-management system" could mean either of two things.

- **Only active case work.** Then meeting time would mostly be excluded. Treated offices cut about 3.3 more hours of meetings than controls, so case-work time would have fallen much less than 11%. A fall of 11% on logs would then be hard to reconcile with a timesheet fall of 12%.
- **All time logged in, including meetings.** Then the log measure is just a near-copy of the timesheets.

This matters for the meetings pathway. If meetings are in the denominator, cutting them raises output per hour fairly directly; output per hour then rises partly because unproductive hours are removed. If they are not in the denominator, the gain must come from more productive case work. Both are real gains, but they mean different things for employers. The measure needs to be defined.

Logs also miss work done off the system: phone calls, paper files, thinking. So "stricter" is true only for on-system work.

### 6. Halden at 24 months: who didn't respond

Of the 23 organisations with output records, 9 did not respond. Non-response may be selective, for example by organisations that reverted or closed. The Halden lead author is also a co-author, which is worth noting. The report itself is appropriately self-critical, though.

One of the three reversions was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. That is not coverage-bound in the meta-analysis's sense. It suggests a third category, deadline-bound client work, which the meta-analysis's two-way coding would miss.

### 7. Still missing

- **Cost per case in case-processing.** Timesheets include claimed overtime. If it was paid, the cost of the scheme goes beyond "full pay." The county measured cost for the counter arm but not here.
- **Backlog size and case age.** These were not reported at either point. They are the direct test of whether "output maintained" hides harder cases being put off.
- **Output per FTE is slowly drifting down.** It went from −2.1% to −3.4%. The interval still includes zero, but the trend is worth watching.

## Where this leaves the debate

| Claim | Status after this report |
|---|---|
| Halden: +23.4%, sector-general | Not supported. Inflated by scheduled hours and manager ratings; fails in coverage-bound work |
| Varga–Holm: entirely an artifact | Not supported. +8.5% on logs at 24 months, randomised and record-based |
| Meta-analysis: no decay | Not supported. Its long studies were weak designs; the within-trial decline is about a fifth to a quarter, partly confounded by contamination |
| Meetings as a mechanism | Supported, not confirmed. Pre-specified, about half the gain, but 7 non-randomised treated offices |
| Coverage-bound work | Settled for this setting. Worse service or about 9% higher cost per contact |

The question that matters most for policy is the one the report correctly says it cannot answer. Could reorganising without cutting hours capture the meetings share of the gain? Or is the cut in hours what forces reorganisation and makes it last?

The two control offices hint at the first: a 4% gain from a smaller cut in meetings. But the evidence is two offices with no comparison group. A three-arm trial would answer this directly: reduced hours, reorganisation only, and control. It is the natural next study.
